# Working with Factors

## Load libraries

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(dplyr)
```

## Import data

```{r}
income_mean <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/master/data/2021/2021-02-09/income_mean.csv")
```

## What is a factor?

A factor is a specialized version of a character — it is how R truly stores categorical data.

- The values a factor can take are called levels
- Levels let you control the order of categories in plots and summaries
- The default order of levels is always alphabetical
- Under the hood, R stores factors as integers (1, 2, 3…) mapped to level labels

```{r}
fruits <- factor(c("Apple", "Grape", "Banana"))
fruits
```

## Factor Booby-Traps

Imagine a column of numbers that has a single typo — R reads the whole thing as characters. If you then convert to numeric, real text becomes NA:

```{r}
test <- c("A", "1", "2")
as.numeric(test)
```

Now try converting after converting to a factor first — this is even worse:

```{r}
test <- factor(test)
as.numeric(test)    # returns the underlying integer codes, not the original values!
```

### Read in data safely

Factor booby-traps are why there was a push to stop importing strings as factors automatically. Always use read_csv() from {readr}. You then convert to factors intentionally and explicitly, only when you need a specific ordering — not by accident on import.

- read.csv() — base R
  - Strings become factors automatically
- read_csv() — tidyverse
  - Strings stay as characters

# The {forcats} Package

**For cat**egorical data — also an anagram of “factors”. All main functions start with **fct\_**

### StarWars data

```{r}
glimpse(starwars)
```

How many of each species?

```{r}
starwars |>
  filter(!is.na(species)) |>   # remove NAs
  count(species, sort = TRUE)
```

## fct_lump() — Lump Rare Levels Together

There are 38 unique species, but most appear only once. Let’s lump the rare ones together. **fct_lump(x, n)** keeps the n most common levels and collapses everything else into "Other":

```{r}
star_counts <- starwars |>
  filter(!is.na(species)) |>
  mutate(species = fct_lump(species, n = 3)) |>
  count(species)

star_counts
```

The result is now a factor — notice the output is no longer alphabetical. The order is determined by the factor levels, not the label names.

## Reordering Factors

The default alphabetical order is almost never what you want in a plot. Start with a basic Bar Plot.

```{r}
star_counts |>
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = n)) +
  geom_col()
```

This is hard to read. It would be more useful sorted by count.

### fct_reorder() — Sort by Another Variable

**fct_reorder(f, x)** reorders the levels of factor f by the values of x:

```{r}
star_counts |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(species, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col()
```

### fct_reorder() — Descending Order

Add **.desc = TRUE** to flip the order:

```{r}
star_counts |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(species, n, .desc = TRUE), y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Species")
```

## Reordering Line Plot Legends

The income_mean Data

```{r}
glimpse(income_mean)
```

### Summarize by Year and Quintile

```{r}
total_income <- income_mean |>
  group_by(year, income_quintile) |>
  summarise(income_dollars_sum = sum(income_dollars), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(income_quintile = factor(income_quintile)) # converts the character column to a factor so we can reorder it
```

**mutate(income_quintile = factor(income_quintile))** converts the character column to a factor so we can reorder it. If you skip this step, **{forcats}** reordering functions won’t work.

### Basic Line Plot — Legend in Wrong Order

The legend order doesn’t match the line order — the highest income group is at the bottom of the legend.

```{r}
total_income |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = income_dollars_sum,
             color = income_quintile)) +
  geom_line()
```

### fct_reorder2() — Reorder by Two Variables

fct_reorder2(f, x, y) reorders f by the values of y at the largest values of x. This aligns the legend with the right end of the lines:

```{r}
total_income |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = income_dollars_sum,
             color = fct_reorder2(income_quintile, year, income_dollars_sum))) + # reorder
  geom_line() +
  labs(color = "income quintile")
```

## Setting Levels Manually

Sometimes you need a specific order that isn’t determined by the data.

### factor() with levels = …

Use the **levels** argument inside **factor()** to set the exact order you want. This is especially useful for months, tide heights, treatment levels — any categorical variable with a meaningful inherent order that isn’t alphabetical.

#### Without levels — alphabetical by default

```{r}
# Without levels — alphabetical by default
x1 <- factor(c("Jan", "Mar", "Apr", "Dec"))
x1
```

#### With levels — your specified order

```{r}
x1 <- factor(c("Jan", "Mar", "Apr", "Dec"),
             levels = c("Jan", "Mar", "Apr", "Dec"))
x1
```

## Subsetting Factors

What happens to factor levels when you filter your data?

### Filter to Common Species

Let’s filter the starwars data to only species with more than 3 individuals:

```{r}
starwars_clean <- starwars |>
  filter(!is.na(species)) |>
  count(species, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species)) |>   # convert to factor
  filter(n > 3)                          # keep only common species

starwars_clean
```

Check the factor levels

```{r}
levels(starwars_clean$species)   # check the factor levels
```

### droplevels() — Remove Unused Levels

**droplevels() (base R)** or **fct_drop() (forcats)** removes any levels that no longer appear in the data:

```{r}
starwars_clean <- starwars |>
  filter(!is.na(species)) |>
  count(species, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species)) |>
  filter(n > 3) |>
  droplevels()                           # remove unused levels
```

Check factor levels

```{r}
levels(starwars_clean$species)
```

### fct_recode() — Rename Levels

**fct_recode(f, “new name” = “old name”)** renames one or more levels:

```{r}
starwars_clean <- starwars |>
  filter(!is.na(species)) |>
  count(species, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species)) |>
  filter(n > 3) |>
  droplevels() |>
  mutate(species = fct_recode(species, "Humanoid" = "Human")) # renames

starwars_clean
```

## Other Helpful **{forcats}** Functions

| **Function**    |  **What it does**    |
|:----------------|:---------------------|
| fct_relevel()   | Move specific levels to the front |
| fct_rev()       | Reverse the order of levels   |
| fct_collapse()      | Collapse multiple levels into one   |
| fct_na_value_to_level()      | 	Convert NA into an explicit level  |
| fct_infreq()          | Order levels by frequency     |
